verdict.rationale: Both changes have identical production code: they rename the CRM `customer_id` to `customerId` at load time, which follows the README's 'read as delivered' rule, and they route the export lookup through the existing `requireCustomer` so failures follow the documented error convention. The tests are equivalent in what they protect; B's extra index lookup adds nothing beyond its `deepEqual`, while A's small temp-directory helper reads a little cleaner. A's report is a little more precise: it states the exit status 1 / empty stdout behavior and the before/after test counts correctly. B says the CRM customers were indexed under an 'empty ID', when in fact they all collided under `undefined`.
a_issues: Report claims both new tests failed before the fix without saying how that was checked.
b_issues: Report says the CRM customers were looked up under an 'empty ID'; in fact they were all indexed under `undefined`, each overwriting the previous one.
The extra `buildCustomerIndex` assertion in the sources test duplicates what the `deepEqual` already guarantees.

verdict.rationale: Both changes make the same fix: they rename the CRM `customer_id` to `customerId` at load time, and they make the export use `requireCustomer` so the README's error convention holds. Both add equivalent tests. The deciding difference is the report: A says the CRM customers were 'looked up under an empty ID', when in fact they were indexed under `undefined` and overwrote each other. B describes the cause and the README-conformant failure behavior (exit 1, nothing on stdout) accurately.
a_issues: Report says CRM customers were 'looked up under an empty ID'. They were actually all indexed under the key `undefined` and overwrote each other, so the cause is described imprecisely.
b_issues: Sources test checks only the loaded records and not the index lookup. This is a minor gap, since the rest is covered elsewhere.
